claims.text: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys above 900 °C, protective-oxide stability is primarily governed by the effect of X on metal/oxide interfacial lattice matching and stress accommodation.
Si facilitates formation of a dense, coherent Cr-rich oxide.
The oxide formed by the Si-containing alloy may incorporate a silica-like network.
The Si-associated oxide structure minimizes oxide-growth stress and metal/oxide interfacial strain.
Oxides resulting from Mn- or Al-containing CrFeCoNiX alloys lack the enhanced coherency attributed to Si.
The lower oxide coherency in Mn- or Al-containing alloys leads to cracking or spallation.
A silica-like phase or network within the Cr-rich scale acts as a binder that enforces oxide-layer coherence.
Silicon improves lattice matching between the protective Cr-rich oxide and the underlying alloy.
Improved lattice matching reduces growth-induced stresses and prevents oxide-scale cracks and spallation.
Mn- or Al-containing alloys experience higher metal/oxide interfacial stresses because they lack the proposed beneficial Si effect.
Under matched exposures above 900 °C, Si-containing alloys will form more continuous, adherent, and coherent oxide scales with less cracking and spallation than Mn- or Al-containing alloys.
Mn- and Al-containing CrFeCoNiX alloys can serve as the non-Si baselines under otherwise identical exposure conditions.
The proposed mechanism applies to both single-phase and multiphase metallic solid-solution states.
The proposed mechanism applies above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres, including O2-rich or SO2-containing environments.

Failure of the Si-containing alloy to show a statistically significant improvement in oxide continuity, adhesion, and spallation resistance relative to Mn- or Al-containing alloys under identical conditions would falsify the proposed mechanism.
